text: Creusa Disappears During the Escape: When the Dead Point the Living Toward a Future, Have They Also Explained the Past?
Troy has fallen.
The flames are approaching Aeneas's house.
He tells his elderly father to climb onto his shoulders.
With one hand he takes hold of his young son.
His father carries the household gods, because Aeneas has just returned from the killing and cannot yet touch sacred objects.
His wife, Creusa, follows them at a distance.
Aeneas says:
Whatever happens, we will share the same danger and the same deliverance.
It is a scene of flight that will be depicted countless times:
A son carrying his father.
Leading the next generation by the hand.
Bearing the gods and the memory of a city.
Moving from a burning past toward a future still unknown.
But in this picture, Creusa is neither carried nor led by the hand.
She has been placed at the rear, to follow on her own.
Later, she is the one who goes missing.
This does not immediately prove that Aeneas places little value on his wife.
One person cannot carry everyone at once.
His father is old and needs him to bear his weight.
His son is young and needs a hand to hold.
Creusa is an adult who can walk by herself. Having her follow behind may simply be the most practical arrangement for their escape.
The streets of Troy are in chaos. Flames, enemy troops, and screams can force a change of route at any moment.
Any group might be scattered.
So we cannot reason backward from the eventual outcome and conclude:
Aeneas deliberately placed his wife where she would be easiest to lose.
Yet the story still brings different members of the family into his attention in different ways.
His father is on his shoulders.
His son is at his hand.
Creusa is behind him.
What a person can most easily keep track of is often what they are carrying or leading.
“She will keep up” entrusts part of the relationship to the other person, and to the chaos around them.
As they approach the gate, hurried footsteps sound in the darkness.
Anchises sees the flash of enemy armor and cries:
Run! They are coming after us.
In panic, Aeneas leaves the familiar road and makes his way through narrow streets.
He does not know where Creusa stopped.
Did she take a wrong turn?
Sit down from exhaustion?
Or was she suddenly snatched away by fate?
He cannot be sure.
But in his recollection, he admits one very specific thing:
Until he reached the appointed meeting place, he neither looked back for his missing wife nor turned his thoughts behind him.
Only when his father, son, household gods, and the others have finally assembled does he discover:
One person is missing.
Creusa has not come.
Until then, neither her friends nor her child nor her husband had noticed that she was no longer with the group.
This admission means that “the chaos of war” cannot tell the whole story of the loss.
The chaos of war is, of course, its most important condition.
Without the pursuing enemy and the burning city, Creusa would not have been separated from them in this way.
Nor is Aeneas's fear a false excuse.
He must carry his father and protect his child while searching for an escape route amid unfamiliar sounds.
A finite human being in extreme danger cannot look in every direction at once.
But “I could not see everything” and “the person I did not see therefore ceased to be my responsibility” are not the same statement.
Aeneas does not say that he watched over everyone perfectly.
He includes his failure to look back in his own story.
This is not self-condemnation.
Nor is it exoneration.
It is a fact that no heroic pose conceals:
When someone carries too much weight, the person most easily lost may be the one assumed capable of keeping up on their own.
Once Aeneas discovers what has happened, he does not accept the loss.
He entrusts his father, son, and household gods to his companions.
Puts his armor back on.
Returns alone to the city now occupied by the Greek army.
He goes back to the gate.
Back to his home.
Past Priam's palace and the temples.
Through the night, the flames, and the enemy, he calls Creusa's name again and again.
He is willing to face once more all the dangers he has just escaped.
This action must remain part of the account.
Otherwise, the essay would rewrite a separation amid chaos as a calculated abandonment.
Aeneas turned back too late.
But he truly did go back.
Having neglected a relationship earlier does not make every later attempt to repair it false.
Equally, a later willingness to risk his life searching cannot undo the fact that he “did not think of her until the meeting place.”
Both things belong to him.
At last Creusa appears.
Not as his living wife.
But as her true ghost and shade, larger than she was in life.
Aeneas is so terrified that even his voice fails him.
Creusa first restrains his frenzied grief.
She says:
This has not happened without the will of the gods.
The ruler of Olympus does not allow you to take me away from here.
A long exile lies before you. You will cross wide seas and reach Hesperia.
There fertile land, a kingdom, and a royal wife await you.
Weep no more for Creusa.
I will not be taken away to serve as a slave to Greek women.
The great Mother of the Gods keeps me in this land.
Finally, she says:
Farewell.
Keep your love for the son we share.
This farewell gives Aeneas a way to go on.
He need not remain forever among the ruins, searching for someone who cannot return.
Creusa herself explains that she cannot accompany him.
She also places Aeneas's future kingdom, marriage, and exile within divine intention.
Without her words, sailing onward could easily seem like abandoning the dead.
With them, the survivor has the possibility of release.
Through a final wish, the dead can sometimes truly free the living from seeing continued life as a betrayal.
Such release is precious.
But it can also be made to do too much.
If Creusa's entire significance ultimately amounts to this:
Telling Aeneas to pursue his mission without misgivings, and making room for his next wife,
Then she disappears again.
The first time, at the back of the fleeing group.
The second, within an explanation of the hero's future.
The ghost's words are real within the epic's world.
They cannot simply be explained away as a fantasy Aeneas invents to ease his guilt.
Divine intention is not an outer shell that a modern reader may discard at will.
Creusa does indeed say that the gods will not allow her to leave.
She is indeed spared enslavement by the victors.
This gives death a dimension of meaning in the work beyond sheer disaster.
But finding meaning afterward does not make every earlier step right.
An outcome may become part of a larger direction.
It cannot prove, in retrospect:
That every arrangement made before they became separated was the only one fate required.
That the failure to look back no longer needs reflection.
That placing her at the rear was naturally the best plan.
“This later led toward a future” and “nothing in the past remains to be answered for” are not the same statement.
People often come to understand a loss differently through what happens afterward.
After a relationship ends, a new life becomes possible.
A failure forces someone off their original path, only for them later to find a direction that suits them better.
Someone's death leads a survivor to take on new responsibilities and accomplish things they would never have begun before.
These later meanings are not false.
If people were allowed to understand loss only as pure rupture, many lives could not go on.
The problem is that meaning must not become the authority to rewrite the past.
Finding a better life afterward does not prove that the earlier harm was right.
Fulfilling a mission afterward does not prove that the person who was lost ought to have been lost in the first place.
The future can make room for the past.
It cannot rewrite the past as nothing more than material prepared for the future.
Creusa foretells that Aeneas will have a royal wife.
And the whole story of Book 2 is being told by Aeneas to Dido in Carthage.
Dido hears about this future.
She does not yet know that her own life will also become part of the cost of Aeneas's continuing mission.
This narrative setting adds another unease to Creusa's farewell.
Aeneas once lost a wife.
His wife's ghost told him to go on, with another marriage still to come.
Later, he will in turn leave Dido for the sake of a future mission.
This does not make the two relationships the same.
Creusa is dead.
Dido is still alive and understands their relationship differently.
But in telling Creusa's story, Aeneas has already made “not remaining with loss” part of his identity.
That identity will still have to be tested by new relationships.
Three times Aeneas tries to embrace Creusa.
Three times her shade slips through his hands.
Like a light breeze.
Like a winged dream.
These three failures matter greatly.
If the ghost's explanation of his mission had resolved everything, Aeneas would not need to reach out again.
He has clearly heard about divine intention, a kingdom, and a future wife.
Yet his body still wants to bring back the person before him.
This shows the unbridgeable distance that remains between “I know I must go on” and “I am no longer bereft.”
The dead can point toward a future.
That does not make them people who can be held again.
A mission can allow life to continue.
It cannot fill the empty space in an embrace.
Creusa's final request is that he care for the son they share.
In this, she does more than hand her husband over to an imperial future.
In Ascanius, she leaves behind a relationship that still endures.
Aeneas's future responsibilities as a father are not only part of Rome's mission.
They are also a relationship that Creusa explicitly entrusts to him at the end.
Even so, the child cannot become merely a symbol left behind by his dead mother.
He has a future of his own.
The wishes of the dead can give the living direction; they cannot turn the living into nothing but instruments for fulfilling those wishes.
Equally, Aeneas's love for his child cannot fully compensate for the loss Creusa has suffered.
The continuation of one relationship does not mean that another has not ended.
When Aeneas returns to the meeting place, he finds that many more Trojans have gathered.
Men and women have brought their belongings, ready for him to lead them to whatever land he chooses.
At this moment, private loss meets public mission directly.
Having just failed to bring back his wife, he immediately becomes the leader of many survivors.
It is no longer possible to stay and search.
The Greeks control the city gates.
Dawn is breaking.
The whole group needs to leave.
If there were only his personal grief, Aeneas might still wander among the ruins.
The emergence of a community requires him to stop searching.
This does not use public duty to erase his wife.
It shows that there are moments when a survivor truly cannot be responsible to the dead alone.
The living are waiting for him too.
Yet the more real the public need, the easier it becomes for someone already lost to be rapidly consigned to the past.
The hero has to move forward.
The epic must move forward too.
New companions, new lands, new wars, and a future city await.
With her own words, Creusa's ghost all but completes the narrative transition.
The essay's task is not to stop the epic from continuing.
It is to deny that transition the power to turn her entirely into a doorway.
She does not die merely to make it possible for Aeneas to leave Troy.
At least in her own final words, she still cares about not being enslaved and about their shared child, and still calls herself his beloved Creusa.
A character can point a hero toward the future.
And still belong to more than that hero's future.
Is Aeneas, then, responsible?
The answer cannot be simply “yes” or “no.”
He did not deliberately abandon his wife.
In extreme danger, he was responsible for his father, his child, the gods, and their escape route.
When he discovered the separation, he risked his life to return to the city.
The ghost and divine intention explicitly told him that he could not take Creusa away.
These facts limit the grounds for blame.
But he also admits himself:
His wife was placed at the rear.
He did not look back or think of her before reaching the meeting place.
These facts limit the grounds for exoneration.
A mature understanding need not find a person guilty or innocent before acknowledging that both sides exist at once.
Some losses are not the sole responsibility of any one agent.
Yet they still contain decisions that could be questioned further.
The dead pointing the living toward a future is one of the tenderest moments in many stories.
She says:
Stop searching for me.
Go on.
Take care of the child.
Accept a new life.
Such words can release the living from a fidelity they can never fulfill.
But truly honoring the dead does not mean allowing a final utterance to silence every fact about the past.
Her permission to go on does not mean that you need not remember how she was lost.
Her pointing toward the future does not mean that her death is explained by the future alone.
Her blessing of a new relationship does not mean that the old one can be written off as a stage whose mission is complete.
Creusa disappears from the back of the group.
Three times Aeneas cannot hold her.
Finally, he lifts his father onto his back and leaves Troy with his son and the survivors.
This is indeed where the epic must begin.
But perhaps a new mission is truly worth pursuing precisely because it does not demand that every life left behind be written down as nothing more than the cost of reaching the future.
The dead can release the living.
The future can give loss new meaning too.
But however grand the kingdom later becomes, it cannot make the distance over which he failed to look back that night cease ever to have existed.

*Textual basis: Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2, narrated retrospectively in the first person by Aeneas to Dido in Carthage. The focus is on his carrying Anchises, holding Ascanius by the hand, and having Creusa follow at a distance, with a meeting arranged at the old temple of Ceres (approximately Aen. 2.705–729); the confusion of their route as the enemy approaches, Aeneas's discovery that his wife is missing only after he reaches the meeting place, his admission that he had neither looked back nor turned his thoughts toward her, and his subsequent return alone to search the burning city at great risk (approximately 2.730–767); Creusa's true ghost explaining divine intention, the long exile, the kingdom and royal wife in Hesperia, her request that he care for their shared son, and Aeneas's three failed embraces (approximately 2.768–795); and his return to his companions, where he finds more Trojans willing to follow him on a distant journey (approximately 2.796–804). This essay does not question the reality of the ghost and divine intention within the work's world, nor does it allow the later mission automatically to prove that every particular arrangement during the escape has been fully accounted for.*
